title: Traitor behaviour splits opinion as paranoia deepens
description: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode seven of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.Six days is a long time in The Celebrity Traito
body: Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode seven of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.Six days is a long time in The Celebrity Traitors.So it was a relief to be put out of our misery as last Friday's literal yawn-fest came to its slow-burning conclusion; the traitorous trio eventually succeeding in their mission to kill in plain sight.The snoozefest - which involved reluctant traitor James Acaster making faithful Ross Kemp yawn by boring him to tears - meant the paranoid EastEnders star was finally put out of his misery. On learning his fate, the actor turned to Shakespeare - who else?"To thine own self be true," he declared, quoting Polonius from Hamlet. "And I was."As usual at breakfast, the faithfuls seated early mused over who may have been murdered overnight: "If Jerry's not here, I don't think I can handle it," Romesh Ranganathan confessed.Jerry Hall was charmingly late to the party. After everyone had discussed Ross's demise, she piped up in her famous Texan drawl: "Is Ross gone?"As the typical off-the-wall theories began to swirl, Jerry later told Miranda Hart she suspected fellow faithful James Blunt - for the very plausible reason that "his face is redder than a fox's ass at gooseberry time". It's as good a reason as any proffered so far this series.Once the croissant crumbs had been cleared, it was time for a mission that threw the cat among the pigeons - not least because the traitor's lair it took place in "smelled like a litter tray", according to Jerry.Miranda felt there were more complex olfactory notes at play: "A mix of salmon, cheap cologne and crotch." Delightful.The mission involved each player having to build a shield on a plinth in front of them out of 3D jigsaw-type pieces which were buried in troughs in sawdust. Think Krypton Factor meets lucky dip.At three intervals, a bell would ring, and the players all had to stop and put on blindfolds for a few minutes. The traitors could then remove theirs and go about sabotaging the handiwork of anyone they fancied. And while James A revealed he was "starting to have more fun" after murdering poor Ross, if there was a prize for the worst traitor of all time, he would still smash it.He was too scared to take off his blindfold and remove any shield pieces from the faithfuls, leaving the dirty work - and all the risk - to fellow traitors Maya Jama and King Kenny. Suffice to say, they were not impressed."He didn't even lift the blindfold off - I'm speechless," said Maya. James A knew he was in trouble: "I'm aware I'll get a dressing down in the turret but I am the one who killed Grant Mitchell." He wasn't wrong about the telling off. And the fact he completed his own puzzle, earning himself a shield, must have really riled his co-conspirators.To be fair, you could argue he's playing a blinder - there's been very little suspicion of him so far. Three other celebrities also managed to complete their shield puzzles - James B, Joanne McNall and Michael Sheen - but no money was banked after Maya and Kenny panicked and didn't remove any pieces at their last opportunity. But the task at least threw up another bunch of mad theories for the faithfuls to chew over, as they tried to unsuccessfully guess where the floorboard creaking was coming from as two of the traitors tried to creep around the room.It was good news for Romesh at least, whose hay fever saved the day - Sharon Rooney could hear him sniffing constantly next to her so knew he couldn't have been a traitor.Maybe the tickly moustache isn't helping his allergies - and combing it won't make much difference.Ahead of the round table, self-styled "Poundland Poirot" Sharon was living up to her nickname with a red herring theory about a perfume bottle being used to kill someone in plain sight. Ross's murder and the disorienting mission ultimately confused everyone, with the round table being the most random of the series so far. Leigh-Ann Pinnock, Bash Croft, Joanne and Jerry were among the accused, with Jerry - having survived murder overnight - banished for being "a professional pot stirrer. She's "planted more seeds than a farmer's market" – or at least that was Joanne's reasoning.Romesh's deadpan excuse was better: "I've long suspected she preferred Rob (his comedy partner and former contestant Rob Beckett) to me."Once again, the faithfuls were left to rue losing one of their own, with Jerry chastising them as she made her grand exit: "I told you so!"Leigh-Ann still had heat on her after Jerry's banishment, with her bright red - blood red? - leather-look long gloves drawing attention in the kitchen."I said they looked traitorous and villainous," she bemoaned.Back in the turret, as James A predicted, Maya and Kenny were not happy about his lack of action at the mission. "You hung us out to dry!" Maya chastised him.But he redeemed himself somewhat by declaring that he had finally got a taste for villainy."When I killed Ross Kemp in plain sight, I loved it!" James A told a delighted Maya and Kenny.It's only taken him three-quarters of the series to get there but better late than never.

schema.headline: Traitor behaviour splits opinion as paranoia deepens

title: Chancellor says he will cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to £800m
description: The chancellor has announced plans to slash "form-filling and pointless paperwork" to save UK businesses up to £800m. Ministers have said the proposed
body: The chancellor has announced plans to slash "form-filling and pointless paperwork" to save UK businesses up to £800m. Ministers have said the proposed changes in regulations, announced ahead of John Healey's first Budget on Wednesday, will reduce unnecessary bureaucracy for businesses.The move is part of a broader effort in the Budget to offer households and businesses more support amid rising costs.In response to the announcement, the Conservatives said Labour had only made problems worse for businesses."Labour have finally admitted that endless red tape is hammering businesses and killing jobs across the country," shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said.Healey acknowledged British firms are "fed up with form-filling and pointless paperwork" eating into time and money that would be more valuable invested into their businesses. He becomes the latest chancellor to pledge to slash red tape, which he said will allow businesses more "breathing space" to invest and create good jobs.The changes should make compliance guidance easier, and simplify the reporting rules firms have to follow, the Treasury said.Ministers have claimed this will save almost £800m in administrative and tariff costs.Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Healey are expected to meet some business leaders on Friday at No 10 North.Burnham said that it's unfair "pointless bureaucracy gets in the way" of hard-working people building their businesses."If you run a business, you want to spend your time serving your customers, creating jobs and growing your firm, not filling in unnecessary forms," Burnham said.The government has set itself a target of cutting regulation by 25% by the end of the current Parliament.The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) Chief Executive Rain Newton Smith has welcomed the plans, but said the test would be in delivering reform. Meanwhile, the shadow chancellor argued that the employment act had only made "the situation worse and has created a youth jobs emergency". "John Healey must get a grip in his Budget next week. He must back our Conservative plans to cut welfare and cut taxes so we can get Britain working again," he said.

schema.headline: Chancellor says he will cut 'pointless paperwork' to save businesses up to £800m

title: Gianni Infantino: Asian football chief gives Fifa president re-election lift
description: Gianni Infantino's hopes of being re-elected Fifa president have been given a major boost by an endorsement from the head of the Asian Football Confed
body: Gianni Infantino's hopes of being re-elected Fifa president have been given a major boost by an endorsement from the head of the Asian Football Confederation.President Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa Salman told the confederation's Congress in Tokyo - which was attended by Infantino - that "we reaffirm our full commitment, of course, to supporting you as you seek a new mandate as president".Sheikh Salman's backing represents a significant u-turn just two months after he signed a joint letter with the heads of Uefa and Concacaf criticising Infantino over his failed plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors. At the time the three confederations accused him of breaking trust "through deception" over the Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, and "a profound failure of judgement...these are not the qualities football deserves in its leadership."But in what appears to be a blow to the rebellion against Infantino, Sheikh Salman told the meeting in Japan it was time "to move forward"."I've spoken to a lot of members within this continent. I know your feeling and I think your commitment is clear as well. Your support to Gianni is very clear," he added."Yes, we had some issues, we spoke about them in the past, but let's not relate the two things together..."As one Asian family, we are ready to move forward, united in your support, Gianni."Alongside Infantino's power base in Africa and South America, Sheikh Salman's endorsement could be crucial in ensuring the Fifa president secures a fourth and final term. At the election in Rabat in March, Uefa will have 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10.The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed. Potential rivals such as Victor Montagliani, the president of Concacaf, and Uefa chief Aleksander Ceferin have let it be known they are not contenders."You've been doing a fantastic job in AFC in the last 13 years, my dear Salman," Infantino said in an address to the confederation's delegates."You will do fantastically as well for the next how many years you want. And always, always with my full support, with the partnership of Fifa, because we have seen what we have been doing in the last years."Asked later about Sheikh Salman's comments, Infantino said: "I feel great about the AFC's support."At a meeting of Fifa's Council last week, Infantino apologised for his World Cup sell-off plan, but failed to offer a full explanation for how the proposal was devised. He also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn).Uefa has since told Fifa it must release key documents and answer all questions relating to its governance and decision-making by 2 November.

schema.headline: Gianni Infantino: Asian football chief gives Fifa president re-election lift

title: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope
description: Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope.A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood gl
body: Raye has won the 2026 Mercury Prize for her show-stopping second album This Music May Contain Hope.A pop record sprinkled with golden age Hollywood glamour, it beat the likes of Sir Paul McCartney, Olivia Dean and Jade to scoop the £25,000 prize."I couldn't tell you how grateful I am to be holding this," said Raye, clutching her trophy at Newcastle's Utilita Arena. "I'm shaking, I'm jet-lagged, I'm tired. It's all blurry."It is the first time a pop album has won the coveted prize - which recognises the best British or Irish album of the last 12 months - since M People's Elegant Slumming in 1994.Speaking to the BBC afterwards, Raye said she'd "poured everything I had" into the record, which features the global hit song Where Is My Husband?"I made this album not focusing on commercial [success], not focusing on making things cookie-cutter," said the 28-year-old."Some of these songs are seven minutes. They're indulgent. They're maximalist."Across 17 tracks and 73 minutes, the record tells a cinematic story about a relationship that ends in tears on the rainy streets of Paris, then follows our plucky heroine as she dusts off the debris and emerges stronger and more resilient.Along the way, it features both of her grandparents, the soul legend Al Green, four separate orchestras and more than 100 musicians.In the run-up to this year's ceremony, Olivia Dean had been the bookmakers' favourite for her second album, The Art of Loving.An easy-going, soulful collection of love songs, it had already been named album of the year at the Brit Awards and the Mobos, and is widely expected to earn the singer a Grammy nomination in the same category next month.Speaking backstage, the singer said she was overwhelmed by the success."I don't think I've processed it yet, to be honest," she said. "I feel like I'm still in this crazy whirlwind of it all."And maybe, when I take a break over Christmas, I'll reflect on the sofa."Other nominees included the rapper Kojey Radical, Geordie jazz act Knats, and former Little Mix star Jade - who was the first ever X Factor winner to receive a Mercury nomination.The shortlist also included the charity compilation album Help (2), recorded in aid of Warchild, which featured new music and cover versions by artists such as Olivia Rodrigo, Damon Albarn, Depeche Mode and The Last Dinner Party.The tracklist also included nine former Mercury Prize winners: Arctic Monkeys, Young Fathers, Wolf Alice, Pulp, Sampha, Portishead's Beth Gibbons, Arlo Parks, English Teacher and Ezra Collective.Last year, the prize was won by Newcastle singer-songwriter Sam Fender, who donated his £25,000 winnings to grassroots music venues, helping to support up-and-coming songwriters around the UK.

schema.headline: Raye wins the Mercury Prize with This Music May Contain Hope

title: Private care investment needs monitoring, regulator says
description: Private companies buying up care homes for older people in England could undermine the government's plan to create a universal care service, the regul
body: Private companies buying up care homes for older people in England could undermine the government's plan to create a universal care service, the regulator says.The Care Quality Commission's annual report, external highlights how a rising share of the care home market is owned by large firms - the five biggest increased their share by 26% in the last two years, driven by interest from US property investors, and now own one in seven homes.While there can be benefits, there are concerns the trend can lead to higher prices and a reduction in quality.The regulator said rapid changes to the market, including the fragmentation of home help into more smaller services, needed monitoring and clearer planning.The CQC said the changes to at-home care, which covers support to help people wash and dress, could create inefficiencies - nearly a third of these services are providing care to four or fewer people.In contrast, there are few smaller care homes judged important for providing specialist and personalised care.Small care homes have always represented a tiny proportion of the care home market, but over the last 14 years the numbers have fallen significantly, particularly those that combine care with nursing support, which are down by a quarter.The CQC said the funding system remains fragile – people using care services either self-fund or, for the poorest, the state helps to pay for their costs.And in some areas, providers are increasingly turning to self-funders, making it more difficult for councils to buy the care they need for those relying on state help.CQC chief inspector of adult social care Chris Badger said the reshaping of the market was happening "largely by accident rather than design", driven by a combination of economic pressure and the problems some councils were having in buying services for those relying on state-funded care.He said this government's renewed focus on social care – Andy Burnham made it one of his key priorities when he became prime minister – was welcome.But he said it was important the market was "shaped around what's best for people"."A clearer vision is needed," he added.Hugh Alderwick, of the Health Foundation think-tank, said the report by the CQC "lays bare the massive challenges" facing the government."The prime minister's commitment to reforming the sector provides an opportunity to fundamentally redraw the state's offer on social care."But change is needed now to strengthen the fundamentals of the system."Councils need enough funding, the right skills and strong leadership to shape services around people's needs."Prof Martin Green, of Care England, which represents care providers, said: "If the government and regulators are concerned by consolidation in the care sector, they need to take some clear and tangible action to support smaller care home providers."He said changes to employer national insurance contributions, inflation and the rising cost of energy was making smaller homes unviable."Unless we get some real progress in a funding settlement, the trend of smaller homes closing will be a trend that will continue."The Department of Health and Social Care said the report demonstrated the "scale of the challenge this government inherited", but said it was committed to overhauling social care.

schema.headline: Private care investment needs monitoring, regulator says

title: 'I'm 96 and have 15 million followers': The grannies taking over TikTok
description: Image source, Grandma DroniakImage caption, Grandma Droniak pays for her care home fees with the money she makes from brand deals on social media ByYa
body: Image source, Grandma DroniakImage caption, Grandma Droniak pays for her care home fees with the money she makes from brand deals on social media ByYasmin RufoBBC NewsNinety-six-year-old Lillian Droniak, known as Grandma Droniak to her social media followers, went viral in June after claiming her retirement home had threatened to evict her for throwing parties.The home later confirmed the threat, but reached a settlement with Droniak that  allowed her to keep partying – but not supply alcoholic drinks. With 15 million followers, Droniak has turned her personality into a lucrative business, earning enough from social media to cover her nursing home fees of $12,000 (£9,000) a month.The Connecticut grandma is one of many older women finding unexpected fame online, with most of their audiences often young enough to be their grandchildren. From fashion and food to dating and homemaking, they are finding new audiences and, in some cases, a new lease of life.'I'm showing it's not that bad to get old'"I always knew I had it in me to be famous, I just didn't think it would happen in my 90s," Droniak tells me, explaining that her grandson began helping her post videos in 2020, initially out of boredom.She believes her appeal lies in showing younger people that life doesn't stop as you get older."They think old people just sit and stare at a wall but I'm showing it's not that bad to get old. We embrace it, can still have fun and I'm still partying and going out sometimes."Her grandson edits her sponsored content, which includes partnerships with food and beauty brands. As well as paying for her nursing home fees, the money also goes towards a college fund for her great-grandchildren.Despite being recognised by fans in public, she says her fame feels different at the retirement home. "They don't get it as they don't go on TikTok."'I'm very picky about brand deals'On the other side of the Atlantic, there's Viv Truran, an equally cheeky and cheery 82-year-old from Cardiff.She started posting on Instagram after losing her husband and her neighbour suggested filming her colourful outfits.Image source, Viv TruranImage caption, Viv Truran shares her colourful outfits with her more than 800,000 followersNow she makes two videos a day from her bedroom-turned-studio, showing off her clothes, 22 pairs of glasses and two drawers of scarves."I get up in the morning, I never come downstairs until I've done my morning video and I'm very strict about that."She also keeps a notebook tracking her followers and views – and is now on book five.Truran is regularly stopped by strangers, many of them women in their 20s and 30s, who tell her they are "frightened of getting old" and she shows them "it's not that bad".Brands have taken notice too and Truran says she'd "be stupid" not to do deals but is selective.She does a couple of sponsored posts a month, prioritising local brands and charities like Age UK who paid her several thousand for a recent campaign."I've turned down some big deals because it's not my thing. I'm very picky about who I work with, I have to really love the brand."'I cry when people send me messages from around the world'Naomi Baker from influencer marketing agency We Are Social says older creators are attractive to brands as they often have "deeply established, highly loyal" communities with greater purchasing power, which "carries a massive premium".Image source, Nonna GracieImage caption, Nonna Gracie has been dubbed "the internet's Italian grandma"Grace Geramita, 85, has millions of followers who watch her cook recipes she has made for decades.Known as Nonna Gracie, she moved from Italy to the US when she was 18 and worked multiple jobs at once to provide for her two daughters. Now, she earns more than she ever made in a previous job.Her grandson Matthew suggested they start filming her cooking six years ago but Geramita wasn't keen as she knew nothing about social media and doesn't "speak very good English", but the videos took off."I always cry when people send me messages from all around the world," she says. Much of her content is about more than food – she says she wants to pass on the "tradition of bringing family together around the table".'Virtual grandma' for followersBaker from We Are Social says this is part of the appeal of TikTok grannies as they "offer comfort in an uncertain world".Their wholesome content can also act as a "virtual grandma" for followers, she says.Image source, Barbara CostelloImage caption, Barbara Costello says many people see her as the mother or grandmother they never had That's certainly the case for Barbara Costello. The 77-year-old former teacher now shares videos about cooking, cleaning and homemaking skills on her Brunch with Babs accounts.Her followers tell her she reminds them of their own mothers and grandmothers, with some calling her "the mom I never had"."Recently, a university student approached me in a restaurant to tell me my cookbook had helped her through her first year living independently and I was so happy."Costello works with brands but says she has to think carefully about if it's something she wants to put her name on.She says the best part of being a creator is seeing former pupils at her book signings with their own children."It's a full circle moment. I really can't believe this is my life."

schema.headline: 'I'm 96 and have 15 million followers': The grannies taking over TikTok

title: World Treadmill Championship: Where amateurs compete against the elite
description: Among them is British marathon runner Charlotte Purdue."I think it's good to get people into running. 5km is obviously not too far so people can have
body: Among them is British marathon runner Charlotte Purdue."I think it's good to get people into running. 5km is obviously not too far so people can have a shot at it, there's no pressure," she tells BBC Sport.Purdue, who holds the third fastest British female marathon time, believes the treadmill has been long misunderstood."I personally love the treadmill and I've always used it in my training. We've got one at home and I find it easy at home and I really enjoy it."But does she think she's got what it takes to be the first ever treadmill world champion?"It's definitely added motivation," she adds. "But I wish it was a marathon on the treadmill, I think I'd have a better chance!"Runners have until 24 January to complete 5km, for free, at an official Run X centre. They can make multiple attempts, but only their best time will count.There is no official 5km treadmill world record recognised by World Athletics.The men's 5,000m track record is 12 minutes, 35.36 seconds, while the women's is 13:58.06The men's road record for the distance stands at  12:49, with the women's at 13:54.The top 25% of runners in age categories from 18 to 75+ will represent their nation at the regionals, before the 10 best men and women in each category advance to the world finals in Italy next March.The $100,000 prize pool is split between the men's and women's overall podiums, across seven age-group categories. The exact distribution has not been published.There are currently 20 countries taking part and the list of elite runners registered has not yet been disclosed. Organisers hope to entice more participants with wildcard entries to events like the 2027 World Road Running Championships in China.Despite the treadmill sometimes being referred to anecdotally as the 'dreadmill' due to the repetitive and monotonous nature of indoor running, World Athletics president Lord Coe told BBC Sport it's a "great opportunity" to introduce a new audience to running."It's across a whole range of age groups. It's very important that we continue to innovate and it's really important that when we innovate, we use technology that attracts more young people into our sport," he says.The ambition for treadmill running doesn't stop there, with hopes the discipline can also be included in Esport competitions in the next five years."We know there are a lot of long-distance challenges but nothing at that 5km mark which is more accessible and that's the real big starting point," Luke Townsend, education manager at Technogym UK, the co-organisers of the competition, tells BBC Sport.Alongside professionals like Purdue on the treadmills in Southampton were members of the 'She Strides' run club.They usually opt to run together outdoors but wanted to take part in Run X to highlight how important treadmill running is from a safety point of view."Unfortunately, so many women in the winter have to change their routines of running outside because they don't feel safe," says Hollie Thackway, founder of She Strides.With the clocks going back this weekend, many runners will soon be spending more of their training time in the dark.Thackway added: "By being able to run inside on a treadmill, it means you don't have to stop your training, you can still be on a programme, achieve your goals and not stop running altogether through the winter, so I think this event is great to highlight that."

schema.headline: World Treadmill Championship: Where amateurs compete against the elite

title: England v Australia rugby league: What happens in Vegas, stays in Vegas
description: Mention of Las Vegas is enough to send a shiver down the spine of any England women's rugby league supporter.Not because of lost life savings on the s
body: Mention of Las Vegas is enough to send a shiver down the spine of any England women's rugby league supporter.Not because of lost life savings on the slot machines or undercooked food at the buffet, but because England fell to a record 90-4 defeat by Australia at the Allegiant Stadium in Nevada.The meeting between England and Australia in March 2025 had been touted as the first in a three-match Test series. It was meant to be the beginning of a regular Women's Ashes competition between two historic rivals and form a large part of world rugby league's charm offensive in the US.Instead it served up a sobering reminder of the gulf between the Jillaroos  - the winners of the previous three World Cups - and England, who shipped 17 tries in a lopsided affair. The sight of Georgia Roche, who scored England's only try, in tears at the final whistle and being consoled by her opponents only added to the suffering of English fans who made the trip. The outcome also led many to believe the game in the northern hemisphere had reached a new nadir - with England's World Cup prospects almost dismissed out of hand as a result. However, it has also delivered a seismic shift in England head coach Stuart Barrow's thinking. Few of those selected for this tournament bear the scars of that encounter, with a youthful and dynamic squad featuring only six of the team from the Sin City debacle. And Barrow says excitement, not trepidation, is the feeling in the England camp as they get ready to face the World Cup co-hosts in Perth on Saturday (10:05 BST)."The youngsters coming in think that they can do better than what we did last time and I fully back that and believe them as well," Barrow said."I don't think they've [Australia] been beaten internationally for a long time, but that's exciting. "If you're a young player coming into this group and coming to represent your country in a World Cup on the other side of the world, you want to play the best."People were saying, 'do we want to avoid teams?' When you come all this way, you want to pit yourself as an athlete against the best. So there is excitement among the group but they're all very aware and very respectful of who we're playing." While England thrashed Wales 70-6 in their World Cup opener, Barrow acknowledged their preparations to face Australia were dealt a "devastating blow" when Jasmin Strange picked up a serious knee injury in training on Tuesday, ruling her out of the rest of the tournament.The absence of the Sydney Roosters second-row forward will be sharply felt by Barrow's squad as they take on opponents who have lost just once since 2016 and remain the benchmark at international level.And Barrow insists that while their most recent encounter is "buried" and "in the past", he is using the chastening loss to help ensure England's readiness for this competition."We learned a lot from it," he added. "We've built on that through all our training over the last 18 months."We've got some senior players who were in that group at the time and it allows them to talk about what happened in that game to our young group. It allows them to talk about the difficulties, challenges and we can draw on the experience mainly from player to player." With Australia opening their campaign with a 40-0 win over Samoa, Barrow says his side will have to step things up from last weekend. "We came up with some unforced handling errors on first. We weren't at such a high completion rate but our skill with the ball let us get away with that," Barrow added."You don't get that opportunity when you play the world champions. If you're giving cheap ball away, then you're defending. "We've done a lot of work about keeping possession and respecting the ball, but I also think we've got some exciting football in us when we get to the right end of the field to challenge them, so that's our aim."Meanwhile, Australia hooker Keeley Nizza has made it clear they will not take England lightly."We definitely know about the rivalry," Nizza said. "Last year we played them in Vegas and there was a big score, but I think England are a very different team now."Along with heritage player Hope Millard, Barrow's new-look squad contains centre Connie Boyd, who crossed for a hat-trick on her debut. They also have Super League's Woman of Steel Jenna Foubister, 19, and her highly-rated Wigan team-mate Isabel Rowe, who kicked nine conversions alongside a couple of tries to record the highest points tally (26) in a single game by a female England player at a World Cup. Barrow, who has previously called Rowe and Foubister's partnership in the halves "telepathic" also has Huddersfield Giants winger Amelia Brown among his new group. The 22-year-old - a dog groomer by trade - scored two tries against Wales, the second of which went viral on social media after she ran 107 metres to score it."My phone's been popping off, so it just feels good," Brown said."Some of my family don't really understand social media. So they're like: What does this mean? What does that mean? But they're all really happy for me and really proud of me."Barrow added: "You don't get many international tries that look like that, so to do that on your World Cup debut is outstanding. "We want moments like that in our sport and especially the women's game because the one million views [it has had] puts us on the map and hopefully that gets people interested back home in our sport. "So anything like that is amazing. I know that Amelia's been sharing a room with Jasmin Strange all week - who's a social media queen - so she's actually outdone Jasmin this time."

schema.headline: England v Australia rugby league: What happens in Vegas, stays in Vegas

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Prepare for the worst' and 'Covid report fallout'
description: The Sun reports that Thomas Markle,, external the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, is being investigated by police, after a "huge stash" of
body: The Sun reports that Thomas Markle,, external the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex, is being investigated by police, after a "huge stash" of child sex abuse images was allegedly found at his home in the Philippines. The paper reports that the discovery was made by the 82-year-old's son, Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Junior. It says he told detectives that "hundreds, if not thousands" of pictures and videos of young girls were "mixed up with innocent family mementos" in four large boxes. There is no response from Thomas Markle Senior.A number of the papers lead on government warnings about preparing for national emergencies. The Guardian says there is "growing concern", external about the impact of climate change, technological dependency and hostile state threats, with the Daily Telegraph highlighting Britain's reliance, external on undersea cables and a "heavily globalised food supply". But the Daily Mail dismisses the warnings, external, accusing what it calls "Nanny Burnham" of "wasting a fortune on lecturing" the country. Its headline is: "Don't panic."The Times says that the government is to make, external its revived Help to Buy scheme "more generous" by raising the earnings cap on who can qualify. It says first-time buyers outside London with a combined income of up to £110,000 will be able to access the scheme, up from £90,000 pounds. In the capital, the threshold is being raised to £140,00 pounds, from £110,000.The Financial Times says that Nato will allow Ukraine, external to buy weapons, ammunition and equipment through its centralised procurement agency. The paper says this could potentially allow Kyiv to obtain supplies faster and more cheaply, and without having to rely on bilateral negotiations.And reports that the search for the next James Bond is nearing its end are highlighted in the Times, external. It says that among the final contenders are the Slow Horses' star, Jack Lowden; Callum Turner from Masters of the Air; and Josh O'Connor, who played Prince Charles in The Crown. They - along with up to two others - are said to be gathering in London this weekend for screen tests. The paper says the next 007 is set to be recruited before the end of the year.

title: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
description: Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming langua
body: Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out."The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue"."But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented"."It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected, external had been received and was being acted on.Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date."Hacking has been around for many years," he said."The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long."MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today. PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.According to cyber-security firm Wiz, external, which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites. And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X, external on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced."That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday.The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday.But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required.In France, telecommunications company Orange also said, external it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally."The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC Group."A few years ago, attackers might have taken weeks to exploit a vulnerability. Now, it can be days or hours."Hull also highlighted the extent of the task facing developers and engineers working to deal with the issue."Several days into this incident, security professionals might already be dealing with significant burnout," he said, urging a need to "make time to rest, share the workload and look after each other"."Resilience depends on people as much as technology."
