title: Streeting: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies
description: Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber-attacks or state-sponsored terrorism,
body: Members of the public and businesses need to think more about how they would cope with natural disasters, cyber-attacks or state-sponsored terrorism, the defence secretary has said.Wes Streeting warned people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them.He added that the government was launching a "national resilience conversation" to raise awareness, including advice for households like stocking up on food, bottled water and first aid supplies.Streeting also said that cyber incidents - like the recently discovered critical security flaw in the programming language which powers much of the internet - will happen "more and more".Streeting told BBC One's Question Time that the UK is facing a greater threat to the country, "than we have certainly for most, if not all, of my lifetime". Speaking to an audience at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford earlier on Thursday, where it was announced production of tank gun barrels would return to the UK, he spoke of "everyday challenges" facing households.He pointed to wildfires burning this summer and the flooding that is expected this winter.Streeting said the public need to be prepared for "increasingly sophisticated cyber-attacks" on businesses, or supply chain disruption caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists".The defence secretary referenced the critical security flaw in the PHP programming language which has left organisations around the world scrambling to update their systems.In the UK, 32 government services were offline while the potential cyber-security issues were addressed."It's not just from foreign states engaged in espionage or sabotage; it's also organised criminals," Streeting told Question Time. "In this world of AI that we live in... it does also present threats if people are innovating and pushing against conventional [cyber] defences."The government hopes to improve the UK's preparedness for emergencies, such as those caused by increasingly likely severe weather events and cyber-attacks by hostile states.Incidents could leave the public without access to everyday services such as mains water, sewage, phones and the internet.The "Be Ready" campaign, external encourages households to stock up on supplies to survive for three days, including non-perishable food, bottled water, a torch, sleeping bags, and first aid items.It also suggests having a FM radio for updates during outages, and writing down the frequencies of any national or local radio stations you use for news.Asked by a Question Time audience member whether the campaign amounted to scaremongering, Streeting said the government want "people to be alert but not alarmed". He said that there was not a "specific thing we've got in mind" when putting out the advice. But, he added that the supplies on the list "might help you through some power cuts, or might also help you through if... your local shop's subject to a cyber-attack and your card isn't working at the till".Security Minister Dan Jarvis MP said the advice will ensure emergency services can prioritise people who need more support during crises, and hopes it will "improve our resilience as a nation".It follows on from similar campaigns by European countries, like France, Ireland and the Netherlands, where the advice is a "normal part of everyday life", he added.Last month Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said people should prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean.She said the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country", and that households should stock up on food to be more resilient.Her comments came as an National Audit Office (NAO) report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience, and that UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland and Sweden.The government launched its national security strategy last year, which warned that the UK must "actively prepare for the possibility of the UK coming under direct threat, potentially in a wartime scenario".It said the nation was "in an era in which we face confrontation with those who are threatening security", and referred to Russia's war against Ukraine and "Iranian hostile activity on British soil". The government said building national resilience meant reducing reliance on others and ensuring UK supply chains and energy security could be maintained "even in times of crisis".

schema.headline: Streeting: Prepare for supply chain disruption from cyber or climate emergencies

title: Are Man Utd the unmanageable club?
description: The cycle of doom that has ultimately engulfed every Manchester United manager since Sir Alex Ferguson now has the hapless Michael Carrick in its unfo
body: The cycle of doom that has ultimately engulfed every Manchester United manager since Sir Alex Ferguson now has the hapless Michael Carrick in its unforgiving grip.Carrick recreated a familiar scene - the same one acted out by predecessor Ole Gunnar Solskjaer after a 4-1 loss at Watford in November 2021 cost him his job - by raising his hands in apology to supporters who had just seen United humiliated by the same scoreline at Como in the Champions League.Carrick is the seventh full-time manager since Ferguson stepped down in 2013 after winning 38 trophies during 26 years in charge.Since then there have been days of success under Louis van Gaal, Jose Mourinho and Erik ten Hag, and moments of hope, but the final outcome is always the same - dismissal.Carrick will need something miraculous to change that storyline, with results poor and revolt within the dressing room as defender Lisandro Martinez took aim at director of football Jason Wilcox after the Champions League defeat at Atletico Madrid, while captain Bruno Fernandes questioned the tactics in Como.It hints at something rotten in the state of United.So should it really be crestfallen managers standing in front of those disappointed supporters?Can it really be United's managers every time? Should not even more scrutiny now be aimed at those who appointed them, then decided the direction of the club?Have United effectively, through years of decay, decline and appalling decision-making, become the unmanageable club?There have been those seven full-time managers - David Moyes, Van Gaal, Mourinho, Solskjaer, Ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and Carrick. There have also been spells as interims for others such as Ryan Giggs, Ralf Rangnick, Ruud van Nistelrooy and Darren Fletcher.United's leaders, from former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward to the ruling Glazer family and now part-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, have effectively tried every trick in the book to recreate the Ferguson era.And failed miserably.Moyes, an ill-starred appointment led by Ferguson, found the job too big for him after leaving Everton. Van Gaal and Mourinho were tried and trusted operators with stellar track records of success at Europe's superpowers. Solskjaer was effectively the anti-Mourinho without any sort of managerial track record that suggested he would succeed at United, but appointed after a successful spell in temporary charge.Ten Hag got the job on the back of leading a superb young Ajax side to the Champions League semi-final. Amorim was regarded as European coaching's hottest young property when he was lured from Sporting in Lisbon.All ended up sacked. All eventually found the unwieldy beast that is United impossible to tame.Van Gaal won the FA Cup in 2016. Mourinho won the League Cup and the Europa League in 2017. Ten Hag won the FA Cup in 2024 with a landmark win against Manchester City.Slim pickings compared to previous glories.United, however, have not become a bad or dysfunctional club overnight. They have been heading towards this point ever since the succession plan to Ferguson - not easy, admittedly - was botched so badly.Carlo Ancelotti, Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp all felt able to resist the lure of Old Trafford, leading to what should have been red faces all round in December 2019, when they were all managing within 35 miles of each other in the north-west but none were at United.Ancelotti was at Everton, Guardiola was at Manchester City. Klopp was at Liverpool. United had Solskjaer, an over-sentimental choice made on the back of a feelgood interim spell. He lasted less than three years.With every passing day, Carrick looks like Solskjaer Mark II. Carrick is a former fan favourite who did well in temporary charge, but whose previous managerial career was a sacking at Championship club Middlesbrough. Solskjaer shared that same unwanted distinction, sacked by Cardiff City in September 2014 after only nine months in charge as they struggled in the Championship.It has all brought United to the point where the question must be asked. Since Ferguson's departure, has it ever been worse than it is now? In recent times, has there ever been less hope than there is now? Has morale ever been lower than it is now?United will always find a manager should they require one, but their current parlous circumstances mean they are no longer the attraction they once were.They will not have the pick of the globe's finest. They will need to persuade someone that there is a future at Old Trafford that contains something other than future dismissal, a sobering state of affairs for the self-styled "biggest club in the world".Given the current state of United's squad, there is no guarantee a manager with a high-class track record would have a quick fix, or any fix at all, without huge investment.Carrick is front of house and, on current evidence, will pay the price for United's failings. He is a repeat of the Solskjaer mistake, an easy choice made after taking them back into the Champions League, a comfort blanket with supporters that has now been torn away by poor results.There are significant culprits elsewhere, led by Ratcliffe.United fans have held regular protests against the Glazers since they took control in 2005, their leveraged purchase loading debt on to the club. They have remained majority owners, despite the level of angered aimed towards them from supporters, unmoved by years of ill feeling.In turn, Ratcliffe's move into part-ownership alongside the Glazer family has meant fans turned on him for his association and business partnership with the hugely unpopular Americans.Ratcliffe, like other successful billionaires before him, has found running a football club is a different world to the one he inhabited previously.He has suggested he leaves big footballing decisions to others, such as Wilcox and chief executive Omar Berrada, but instability and rank bad decisions have come with Ratcliffe as United's leading figure.United were set to sack Ten Hag before the FA Cup final win against City, but the Wembley win earned him an unlikely stay of execution. He was then given a contract extension and £200m in transfer funds, only to be sacked six months later. The pay off to Ten Hag and his staff was more than £10m.It was a catastrophic move to keep Ten Hag, both financially and in a footballing context.Then there was the farce of the pursuit and subsequent sacking of sporting director Dan Ashworth in 2024.He arrived in July with a reputation as one of the game's shrewdest administrators, regarded as a prized capture, only to leave after a behind-the-scenes disagreement five months after his appointment.The impression of a club in chaos, in which United still exists today, was confirmed by the stark fact Ashworth actually spent as long on gardening leave waiting to join from Newcastle United as he did in post at Manchester United.It was suggested Ashworth had been held responsible for Ten Hag staying, but another theory was that he wanted to target English managers such as Graham Potter and Gareth Southgate rather than Amorim.United instead pursued Amorim, whose obsession with a 3-4-3 system had already persuaded Liverpool to look at Arne Slot to succeed Klopp. It was the fault that holed his reign below the waterline.Amorim was gone after 14 months, but not before a parting blast at United's hierarchy and a hostile meeting with Wilcox.Even before Carrick's appointment, morale at Old Trafford had been low after savage cost-cutting under Ratcliffe, with many staff leaving, among other "efficiencies".This season ill feeling among an already dissatisfied fanbase boiled over after United launched a ticket-touting investigation in the summer.Although they admitted to underestimating the number of fans who shared their account details, and toned down some of the threats around season-ticket confiscation if supporters failed to respond as requested, United officials defended the investigation.If the football has been underwhelming, finances - which Ratcliffe promised to improve - still remain an issue.Figures revealed in September confirmed overall debt remains at £1bn, despite Ratcliffe's cost-cutting. United did announce record revenue of £678m and a £23m operating profit despite not playing in Europe for the first time in a decade. This represented a huge shift from the £113m loss in 2023-24.United also confirmed spending £64m buying land for the new stadium, which Ratcliffe hopes can be his legacy at the club and proof of his desire for success.In August Berrada said the club remained on track to build the projected 100,000-capacity stadium at an estimated cost of more than £2bn.However, it is the record of bad decisions backstage and lack of success on the pitch  that is the unpalatable cocktail currently poisoning United.It leaves them facing the possibility of more churn and instability as the clubs they would regard as competitors threaten to become a spot in the distance.

schema.headline: Are Man Utd the unmanageable club?

title: Met detective raped by fellow officer says police handling 'like being raped all over again'
description: A Metropolitan Police detective, who was raped by a fellow officer, has told the BBC that Scotland Yard's handling of her case was "like being raped a
body: A Metropolitan Police detective, who was raped by a fellow officer, has told the BBC that Scotland Yard's handling of her case was "like being raped all over again".Det Con Linda Williams was attacked in 2004 by PC David Carrick - a serial abuser jailed for life in 2023 for sexual offences against her and 11 other women.Linda has post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) because of the attack and sought damages from the Met for failing to protect her from Carrick. The lengthy civil case left her feeling suicidal, she says.The "worst thing", she says, was when lawyers acting for the Met commissioner challenged the severity of her PTSD on the basis that she had been raped only once.The Met has told the BBC it "tried to reduce further distress and re-traumatisation to DC Williams' welfare and has aimed to deal with her claims as quickly and compassionately as possible"."We recognise the unique and additional impact on DC Linda Williams, whose exposure to Carrick came as a result of her being a Met officer," the force added. "Her continued commitment to public service, in spite of the trauma she experienced, is commendable."Linda, who has waived her legal right to anonymity to speak to the BBC, has settled her civil case and the Met has now paid her compensation without acceptance of liability.In an unprecedented move for a serving officer, she is now calling publicly for Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley to resign. She believes he has failed to change police culture as promised and she still does not trust her own force to handle cases like hers.When he took on the most important job in UK policing in 2022, Sir Mark pledged to change the Met. At the time, the force was viewed as being in crisis - following Sarah Everard's murder by a serving officer and other scandals including officers sharing photos of murdered sisters Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman.After Carrick was jailed in January 2023, Sir Mark praised the victims and said: "We have failed and I'm sorry. He should not have been a police officer." Two months later, in an official report by Baroness Casey, the Met was described as a "boys' club", that was institutionally misogynistic and had failed women.Linda contacted the BBC, after seeing Panorama's report last year into a hidden culture of misogyny and racism inside the Met.Since reporting the rape by Carrick in 2021, Linda says it has been "horrific" and she would not report a rape to the Met today "because I don't trust the police and I don't think they deal with it correctly".Carrick was brought to justice by Hertfordshire Police, which investigated the rape of Linda. She reported it to the force after seeing media coverage of the news that Carrick had been charged with raping another woman.Linda was herself a rape investigation officer in the early 2000s."I supported victims through rape but didn't report myself. I think that says loads."I'm asking members of the public to report, and I'm there to support them, but I wouldn't do it myself and I didn't do it."She says if a similar attack happened to her tomorrow, she would not report it to the Met, because she has "no faith" that the force would deal with it correctly.Carrick raped her while she was on a three-month attachment with him in south London - miles from where she was normally based.One night, Linda says, Carrick suggested she should stay at his home, so she did not have to drive far late at night only to return early the next morning.He then raped her.When Linda told him no, she says Carrick replied: "It's what I do. I'm going to carry on."She knew that if she fought back then Carrick was going to get violent, she says.Afterwards, Linda says she "never told a soul".She says she felt unable to report the rape then, or for years afterwards, because of the culture in the Met.Reporting the rape "would have been the end of my career", she says, because Carrick would not have been charged and she would have been shunned."I would imagine that if Carrick had been arrested, he probably would have been interviewed and then no further action. So then mud sticks, doesn't it?"Then I'd be the officer that alleges rape, and who's going to want to work with me?"The "very sexist" culture she says she experienced included having her forehead stamped with the words "Property of the Met" and being locked in the boot of a police car for the duration of a shift.Linda, now 60, says the mental and emotional impact of the rape has been vast.She has led a lonely life, she says, focused primarily on her work and pets. She has not had a relationship with a man since the day she was attacked and says she has missed out on having a family."I still don't feel I could have any relationship," she adds.She feels guilty at not having come forward earlier to report Carrick, she says.Since his conviction, she says the Met's culture has not changed as much as it should have done."We've not moved on enough in the police to really give victims of domestic violence, sexual offences any [of the] support they really need."Her PTSD after the attack is "90% down to the Met Police, 10% to Carrick", she says.Linda brought a civil case against the Met seeking damages on the basis the force failed to protect her from him and that she felt she had been unable to report the rape.During the four-year case, she says the Met's legal team questioned the severity of her PTSD diagnosis."I was horrified and shocked," she says, adding she was reduced to tears and felt she was being called a liar.The Met team also suggested her PTSD could not be severe because she had been raped only once, she says."I don't know how many times you have to be raped to have severe PTSD," Linda saysThe BBC has seen a document from the Met, sent to Linda, showing it stated that a key factor in assessing damages was that the "abuse itself was isolated to a single episode".Linda's solicitor, Sophie Bullimore, of Penningtons Manches Cooper, says to see the rape "reduced down on paper to it being a single isolated event, when actually it has impacted every single aspect of her life, it just needs to be handled with more care".If you have been affected by the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action LineLinda says Met lawyers used the fact that she was an exemplary officer, and continued to perform well at work, to suggest she had shown no signs of psychological trauma.This fails to understand trauma, or how it manifests itself, she adds.The Met document, sent to Linda, shows it argued that - for at least 15 years after she had been raped - the psychological harm she experienced was "not such as to significantly impact her on a day-to-day basis".The Met's legal approach, says Linda, felt "like being raped all over again" - with the force controlling the process and deciding what she was worth.The lawyers were acting on behalf of the commissioner, whom she therefore regards as being personally responsible.At the time of Carrick's conviction, Sir Mark publicly apologised to the 12 victims. Linda says she waited a couple of months to see if he would get in touch with her directly.When she did not hear anything, she emailed, telling him that as "a serving officer, one of his troops, maybe I thought he would come forward and speak to me".He did then meet her, she says, and "said he was sorry". But the apology lacked detail, she says, so it "meant nothing".The commissioner lacks empathy and is more concerned with public perception than supporting victims or officers, she tells the BBC."I would like him to resign. I don't think he's fit for the job."My colleagues have been really supportive and absolutely fantastic, but the support from higher management isn't there."Sir Mark has "repeatedly acknowledged" that Linda has shown courage in speaking out about her experience to drive forward necessary change and, in now waiving her anonymity, to continue to do so, said the Met spokesperson.The commissioner has "contacted DC Williams to ask whether she would be willing to meet again and further discuss these issues in person", they added.But Linda is not convinced."I'm speaking out now because I want to help other victims, whether they're police officers, police staff or members of the public."We can turn it around, but I don't think Mark Rowley can turn it around."If you are you affected by the issues in this story, or you have other information you would like to pass on, get in contact by email daniel.desimone@bbc.co.uk or via the Signal messaging app @investigation.56

schema.headline: Met detective raped by fellow officer says police handling 'like being raped all over again'

title: Dream night for Bournemouth - how did the Premier League come to dominate Europe?
description: At times, being a Bournemouth fan must feel like living in a simulation.That was certainly the case on Thursday night as the Cherries beat seven-time
body: At times, being a Bournemouth fan must feel like living in a simulation.That was certainly the case on Thursday night as the Cherries beat seven-time continental champions AC Milan 3-0 in only their third-ever European fixture.Justin Kluivert scored the opener at Vitality Stadium, 31 years after his father, Patrick, scored the winning goal for Ajax against Milan in the Champions League final.Having seen their club narrowly avoid the jaws of liquidation in 2008, not many Bournemouth fans would have dreamed that famous name would one day appear on their shirts."It's mega. In terms of the story of the club it's ridiculous. Someone told me today, 15 years ago today we were 17th in League One, so it's pretty incredible," Bournemouth midfielder Ryan Christie told TNT Sports."So many of these fans have been here for this journey so to have nights like this and win as well is special."To add to the peculiarity of the situation, Milan fielded more English players in their starting XI (three) than the hosts (two).While the sending off of Milan goalkeeper Mike Maignan killed the contest after 27 minutes, Bournemouth were by far the better side up until that point.In truth, that didn't come as a surprise, even though Bournemouth have won just six points from seven league games this term while Milan are fourth in Serie A.The three sides they have beaten this season - Real Sociedad, Sturm Graz, and now Milan - have all competed in the Champions League inside the past three years.For them it's a fairytale, but for the rest of Europe, is it a Premier League-induced nightmare?Five months after a missed Arsenal penalty denied a Premier League clean sweep in the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League, is this yet another sign of English club dominance?English clubs played nine games in Europe this week, losing just once.In fact, Premier League clubs have lost just four of 26 games played across the three continental competitions so far this season. Manchester United are responsible for two of them.In the five seasons since the Conference League was introduced, no league has yet won all three, but in three different seasons Premier League clubs have won two of them.Over the past two seasons, Premier League clubs have played 21 knockout ties against European opposition in the Conference League and Europa League - and won all 21.The only two ties they have lost have been to other English teams.But, despite such dominance, the Champions League still remains elusive for most, with only Manchester City lifting the trophy over the past five years.So, why are English clubs so dominant in Europe's secondary competitions - and why hasn't this transferred to consistent Champions League glory?Fifteen of last season's 20 Premier League teams featured in the top 30 of Deloitte's 2026 Money List.It is easy to see why then English clubs appear to be head and shoulders above the rest when it comes to the Europa League and the Conference League.Premier League clubs earn more than £1.37bn per season in television rights, a figure La Liga, Serie A, Bundesliga and Ligue 1 could only match combined.Brighton are easily the richest club in the Conference League this season, while Bournemouth and Crystal Palace both appear in last season's top 30.Last season Aston Villa beat Freiburg comfortably in the Europa League final, with a revenue more than double the Germans'.Crystal Palace won the Conference League with a revenue of almost four times more than Rayo Vallecano, the side they saw off in the final.In 2025, Tottenham beat Manchester United in the Europa League final. In the Premier League, they finished 17th and 15th respectively.In 2022-23, West Ham finished 14th and won the Conference League.All the evidence points to the Premier League's collective strength. Take away Europe's richest and England dominates.The summer transfer window was further evidence of Europe's struggles against the Premier League, with the latter again setting a new transfer spend record of £3.49bn to dwarf their rival leagues.Of the 20 most expensive transfers completed in the summer only six were not to clubs in the English top flight.You now have Premier League clubs - away from the traditional big six - beating other top European sides to signings.Premier League wages are generally higher and the league is increasingly seen as the place to be for a lot of European talent."With the exception of some of the global brands within football, and I think you'd look at Real Madrid, Barcelona, PSG and Bayern Munich, the Premier League can outspend anyone and everyone," football finance expert Kieran Maguire said in August."A significant proportion of overseas players are now choosing to play in England than elsewhere in Europe because of the wages on offer."Despite the success of Premier League sides in the Europa League and Conference League, the Champions League is a harder nut to crack.While Barcelona, Real Madrid and Bayern Munich all lost to English teams in last season's elongated Champions League league stage, it has been a very different story when it really mattered.Over the past two campaigns, eight of nine English teams have been knocked out by one of the Deloitte Money League's big four, according to the last report produced in January 2026.Chelsea, Manchester City, Newcastle and Liverpool were eliminated by an aggregate score of 25-6 last season.No English club appeared in the top four of Deloitte's Money List, with Real Madrid, Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain leading the way. Three of those have won the Champions League five times between them in the last seven years.English clubs are certainly very much in the mix for the Champions League, with Arsenal losing last season's final on penalties and Manchester City winning in 2023.But, with just one English club in the past three finals, the Premier League elite are yet to take their European domination to the very top.Come May, it could well be Bournemouth, Brighton, Crystal Palace or Sunderland leading the English charge in Europe.

schema.headline: Dream night for Bournemouth - how did the Premier League come to dominate Europe?

title: The great Ballon d'Or campaign - a race for football's biggest individual prize
description: An emotional Ousmane Dembele had barely settled back into his chair at Paris' historic Theatre du Chatelet last September, gold-dipped orb in hand, wh
body: An emotional Ousmane Dembele had barely settled back into his chair at Paris' historic Theatre du Chatelet last September, gold-dipped orb in hand, when campaigns for this year's men's Ballon d'Or prize began to whirr into action.Entourages roused their candidates, media revelled in the hype. Who deserved the award in 2026? A World Cup year, no less, in which the narrative occasionally became not just which players could lead their country to glory, but how doing so would help them secure football's biggest individual accolade."The Ballon d'Or has been discussed every single day," said European football expert Guillem Balague on BBC Sport's Euro Leagues podcast."Quite clearly it follows the pattern of society, where it puts a lot of emphasis on the individual - it's harder to understand why a collective works, it becomes very easy to understand why one dribbles or doesn't dribble."Clamour for the spotlight only increased as the red-carpet ceremony neared."You can't underestimate the PR machine that some clubs and some players are going to use," added French football journalist Julien Laurens.Managers and sporting directors talked up their charges, and questioned why others on their squad did not make the 30-man shortlist.Deco branded it a "huge scandal" that Barcelona pair Raphinha and Pedri missed out, but backed Lamine Yamal as overwhelming favourite to win it. Not, he says, because he is also a Barca player, but "because I like football".Star names have appeared frequently in the media. Lamine Yamal himself insisted he will not "beg for anything" - after last year saying he dreamed of "winning many" - but suggested the prize should not merely go to the top goalscorer.Paris St-Germain manager Luis Enrique confessed he is "bored of the Ballon d’Or" - although with a record 10 PSG players on the shortlist, perhaps he wishes to keep out of the debate. Dembele and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia talked each other up to BBC Sport."We can cut it in two," joked Dembele. "Honestly, he deserves it, the season he had was exceptional." Kvaratskhelia responded: "Of course it's him!"A 'Kvara d'Or' campaign in Georgia celebrated the country's favourite fleet-footed son."I think for the big nations it's really difficult to understand what [winning] would mean for the small country," the winger explained.Kylian Mbappe, who Real Madrid boss Jose Mourinho compared to the original Ronaldo, was less subtle than most in his pitch to win the award for the first time."I always think I'm the best but everyone has their own opinion," professed the Frenchman, now the all-time World Cup top goalscorer. "Of course, this year could be good for me to win the Ballon d'Or - but journalists vote."Indeed - since a short spell of national team captains and managers also voting ended in 2015 - the 30-player shortlist drawn up by the publications France Football and L'Equipe has been voted on by one journalist from each of the top 100 Fifa-ranked nations.The deadline has passed. The winner has already been chosen.James Kirkham, a sports brand strategist who has worked with top clubs and players, including Harry Kane, says the build-up has had an election feel. "You're going out, canvassing, getting your vote and making sure you shore up certain blocks from certain countries, and why wouldn't you?" adds Kirkham.The lobbying is not for everyone. Max Eberl, Bayern Munich's board member for sport, championed Kane and Michael Olise but said the best players, external "are the ones who don't need to run a campaign". Mbappe's compatriot, Jean-Pierre Papin, winner of the award in 1991, meanwhile told French TV:, external "I like Kylian a lot, he's a record-breaker. However, there comes a point when it's all about me, me, me and me."Mbappe did make an interesting observation, alluding to the dominance of Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo - the pair won a combined 13 in a 15-year period between 2008 and 2023."My idea of the Ballon d'Or comes from the Messi and Ronaldo era - you don't give it to ordinary players, you give it ​to players who are different," explained Mbappe.AC Milan's Kaka was the last recipient before Messi and Ronaldo's tug-of-war began, the Brazilian pipping the young pair to the prize in 2007.That was a year after fledgling social media platforms Facebook and Twitter launched to the public. Nokia dominated mobile phone markets, people took digital cameras on nights out.The world had changed immeasurably by the time Messi won for an eighth time in 2023."Today everything moves at the speed of light," explains former AC Milan chief executive and sporting director Ariedo Braida, who witnessed the club land seven awards, from Ruud Gullit to Marco van Basten's treble, George Weah, Andriy Shevchenko and Kaka."Fans follow individuals - the players - rather than the club themselves. It's a widespread phenomenon, which we see, for example, in politics too."Once upon a time, you'd be a Milan fan and go to watch Milan. Today, everything is live and with the Champions League you always get to see all the great stars straight away."I must say this makes me feel a bit nostalgic, because the event is always immediate. Anticipation creates that sense of longing which has now disappeared."Messi and Ronaldo's brilliance, and often tribal online following, has also driven an increased emphasis on individual records - among fans, media and the players who grew up dreaming of emulating them."You could argue we are in a more interesting time because for basically 15 years it was Messi v Ronaldo and it certainly feels more open. It is a different play now," adds Kirkham."The social noise is deafening, relentless, all-consuming - every fan has an insatiable appetite, every point is riffed on, reacted to, but you also have this domino effect in microcosms of the media on every platform."Clips go viral - a great goal, magical piece of skill, a dazzling dribble - but so do opinions."Now a solitary word on a broadcast can get played out as tweets, reacted to by creators and ex-players in video content that exists on reels and shorts and stories, that gets back-played through radio and on TV screens," adds Kirkham."It's the whole ecosystem, the manner in which it amplifies across these different spaces and platforms, then it generates narratives."No-one is doing anything wrong, creating something they believe is resonating with their audience. But en masse that is a machine, a fierce output that is generated for a player or against a player or whatever that may be."Braida, who was at Barcelona when Messi won the 2015 prize, would agree: "These days, media exposure is absolutely crucial. With the advent of social media, the world has changed radically compared to my day."There's been a global transformation, and today we live in a small global village, because with the internet you can reach everywhere in real time."Michael Owen tells a story about how when Liverpool boss Gerard Houllier rang to break the news he had won the award in 2001, the 22-year-old did not even know what the Ballon d'Or was.Owen engaged in a photoshoot at Liverpool's Melwood training ground a fortnight before the images were distributed to the media, with the striker officially presented the trophy on the Anfield pitch before a game against Derby County.He was the first winner playing for an English club since Manchester United's George Best in 1968, the period in between dominated by Italian, Spanish and German teams.From its launch in 1956 until 1995, when Weah became the first and so-far only African player to win it, only European players were eligible.Only in 2007 did the award became truly global, open to players from any club - not just those representing European teams. Not until 2011 was it awarded at a glamorous ceremony. And only in 2018 was the women's prize launched. "Winning the Ballon d'Or has an extremely positive impact," adds Braida. "We at AC Milan bought Kaka for around 7.5m euros and sold him for 67m euros [to Real Madrid]."I must tell you, however, that in 2008, following his Ballon d'Or win in 2007, Manchester City made us a written offer of 105m euros. We're talking about a written offer, not a sounding-out or mere words."We were probably still in the early stages of certain commercial developments at that time, but now it clearly has a massive impact. Even back then, his value increased fivefold and winning the Ballon d'Or brought him global exposure and fame."For someone like Three Lions captain Kane, hoping to become the first English winner in 25 years and only the fifth of all time, the prestige is huge - especially with the ceremony held in London to mark the 70th anniversary of Stanley Matthews winning the inaugural prize."It would be a massive achievement if it did happen," Kane said on Wednesday, having remained coy on his own chances.Kane has done his share of recent interviews but others, such as Rio Ferdinand on Bayern's official social accounts, have made his case for him. "Ballon d'Or!"He is, after all, vying to become Bayern's first winner since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge's second successive triumph in 1981. Not since Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer 30 years ago has it returned to the Bundesliga.Bayern will also remember the case of Robert Lewandowski, who was widely tipped as favourite in 2020, scoring at an astonishing rate as the Bavarians won all six trophies available, including the Champions League, before the ceremony was cancelled because of the Covid-19 pandemic.The Poland striker, who finished runner-up to Messi the following season, told BBC Sport last year the prize has become "part football, partly politics" and was "more commercial" than its counterpart, The Best Fifa Men's Player award.Ballon d'Or snubs can cut deep. Franck Ribery said it felt "like a robbery" when he missed out to Ronaldo in 2013. Real Madrid boycotted the 2024 ceremony when they learned Manchester City midfielder Rodri would scoop the gong instead of Vinicius Junior."In Brazil, the hype is also giant," explains Caique Andrade, international football reporter at Globo. "When Vini didn't win the 2024 Ballon d'Or, there was a lot of commotion about it."It may be an individual award, but winning is huge for clubs, too."This means an incredible impact in terms of popularity, visibility and also financial returns for the club," explains Braida. "Today, with the rise of social media and followers - factors that shape commercial aspects - this is even more true."Kirkham concludes: "It is a global point - that means more audience and more eyeballs, and that means more money around the world."

schema.headline: The great Ballon d'Or campaign - a race for football's biggest individual prize
